predictions.title: Hugging Face's downloader ships no default XET-to-HTTP fallback by Q2 2027
predictions.body:
Alibaba took Qwen3.8-Max generally available on Monday, August 3 at 2.4 trillion total parameters with roughly 95 billion active per token, and said it will open the weights next week alongside a smaller Qwen3.8-27B. The same day, Unsloth published 2026.8.2 to PyPI, one release after 2026.8.1, and the substance of it was not a kernel and not a new model family. Downloads now fall back automatically from XET, the transfer path Hugging Face uses in place of a plain file pull for large repositories, to ordinary HTTP when XET stalls, with transfer memory much reduced. The release note is one line: "Unsloth now auto fallbacks to HTTP if XET stalls." A project whose reason to exist is making training fit on smaller hardware spent a release making a download finish.

The prediction is about where that fix does not travel. Through the close of Q2 2027, huggingface_hub's default download path still does not recover a stalled XET transfer by finishing the same file over plain HTTP. Recovery work stays inside XET — more retries, better stall detection, chunk-level resume, faster delivery infrastructure — and the cross-protocol bail-out stays where Unsloth put it, in the project holding the file.

Today the client has no such thing, and the shape of the code says why. The download path decides once, before any bytes move: if the repository is XET-backed and the hf_xet package is present it calls the XET getter, otherwise it calls the HTTP getter, and there is no handler between them that could move a file from the first to the second mid-flight. The one place the path uses the word fallback is a warning aimed at a machine where hf_xet was never installed — XET is enabled for the repository, the package is missing, so it is falling back to regular HTTP download. That is a fallback for a client that never had the fast path, not for a transfer that lost it. HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET expresses the same limit: it changes which path is chosen, not what happens when the chosen path dies.

The failure it would guard against is not hypothetical. Two open reports on huggingface_hub's own tracker say so. Issue #4520, filed on July 11, has progress bars and the XET log simply ceasing to update on a large pull. Issue #4349, filed on June 12, is the detail that makes a fallback harder than it sounds: with XET already disabled, the plain HTTP path has no automatic retry of its own, dying at 17.3 of 42.5 gigabytes with nothing left in the cache to resume from. The escape hatch is not obviously more reliable than the thing it escapes.

The force holding the fix inside XET is that XET is the product, not a transport detail. It is the path Hugging Face built to replace an ordinary file pull for exactly these repositories, and a default that abandons it the moment it stalls does three things at once: it concedes in shipped code that the storage layer cannot be trusted with the artefacts it was built for, it throws away whatever partial state the transfer had and restarts the file whole on a slower route, and it removes the pressure that produces the real fix. Vendors ship the retry. They do not usually ship the admission.

Scale is what turns an annoyance into a structural gap. Kimi K3's published weights ran to 1.56 terabytes across 96 shards; a 2.4-trillion-parameter artefact sits in the same class, and the 27B sibling shipping beside it is a statement about who the flagship is actually for. At that size a pull is not a click but a job that runs for hours over a link that will drop at least once, and the chance of a clean first attempt falls with every shard. The parties absorbing that are not individuals pulling weights onto one machine — they are the intermediaries who fetch the reference weights once and republish something smaller, which is the population Unsloth serves and the reason its release notes have started to read like a transfer library's.

What settles this is a shipped version, not a roadmap. The prediction is wrong if, on or before the close of Q2 2027, a released huggingface_hub detects a stalled or failed XET transfer and completes that same file over the plain HTTP endpoint with no environment variable set and no exception handling written by the caller, visible in the release notes or in the download path itself. Three things do not count against it. More retries, better stall detection, chunk-level resume or faster infrastructure inside XET are the predicted outcome rather than its negation. A friendlier HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET is still a decision taken before the first byte moves. And further downstream projects shipping their own bail-out — a serving runtime, a local runner, a mirror — confirm the claim rather than break it, because the point is that this keeps being written by whoever is receiving the file rather than by whoever is sending it.

reasoning.because: Unsloth 2026.8.2 auto-falls back to HTTP when XET stalls; huggingface_hub has no equivalent
reasoning.given: XET is Hugging Face's own storage path; a default exit to plain HTTP concedes it fails at scale
reasoning.so_that: Stall recovery stays inside XET as retries and resume, while each consuming project writes its own cross-protocol exit
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a shipped huggingface_hub default, no env var and no caller retry
reasoning.plain_language: Downloading giant AI models often stalls, and Hugging Face will keep fixing its own system rather than switching to the plain old download method.

predictions.summary: Unsloth 2026.8.2 adds an automatic fallback from XET to plain HTTP when a download stalls. Hugging Face's own client has no equivalent: it picks its transfer path before the first byte moves. Expect no default cross-protocol fallback in huggingface_hub by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Autonomous-pentest vendors take CREST's AI accreditation by Q2 2027
predictions.body:
Two things happened to autonomous offensive security on the same Monday and they read in opposite directions. Horizon3 announced a 250 million dollar Series E at a valuation above two billion, roughly triple the 650 million dollar valuation it carried out of its Series D in June 2025, co-led by NightDragon and NEA, both already shareholders, and oversubscribed enough to admit seven new investors alongside five returning ones. NightDragon founder Dave DeWalt, who ran FireEye and McAfee before this, took a board seat. The company sells an autonomous penetration-testing platform, says it approached 100 million dollars in annual recurring revenue last year at 120 percent growth, and the pitch it chose for the raise is that offence and defence are both automated now and racing each other. The same day, Microsoft opened Project Perception to public preview inside Defender: red agents that map paths to compromise before an attacker walks them, blue agents that decide what counts as meaningful risk, green agents that take corrective action, handing off to each other automatically instead of parking in a queue for a human between stages, on consumption-based pricing. One company was just priced as a category. The other just watched the capability arrive as a meter on a bill its customers already pay.

The reflex reading is that the second event repriced the first one downward before the ink dried, and that is the wrong place to look. Ask instead what a customer is buying when it buys a penetration test it did not choose to want. A large share of that spend exists because a standard demands it, and the standards do not ask for a capability. The payment-card data security standard asks for a tester who is qualified and organisationally independent, and it names the credentials that qualify one. The federal cloud authorisation programme in the United States asks for an assessor accredited to do the assessing. Neither asks how clever the tooling was. What is being bought is somebody's accountable signature on a document an auditor will accept, and Horizon3 conceded that point long before today. Its own compliance offering for the payment-card standard is delivered by Horizon3's Offensive Security Certified Professionals, human testers who hand the customer a penetration test report and an accompanying fix-action report to share with the auditor of choice, with the autonomous platform running underneath them. The most autonomous company in the category already puts a certified person on the invoice for the part that has to be signed.

Six days before the round, that arrangement stopped being an improvisation and became a standard. On July 28, CREST, the body that accredits penetration-testing firms, published the first AI additions to its accreditation standards and opened applications the same day: a new Domain 7, Responsible AI Use, in the company general requirements, covering governance, oversight and transparency in a provider's organisational use of AI, and a new Annex B, AI-Enabled Penetration Testing, in the penetration testing accreditation standard, written so that AI enhances professional judgement rather than substituting for it. Nobody held it yet, and CREST expected its first accredited organisation within about a month. What that document does is convert the one thing a bundled product cannot supply into something a buyer can put on a purchase order: independently assessed, held by a named company, and about the conduct of the engagement rather than the strength of the tooling. It is the first artefact on this seam that is neither a capability claim nor a benchmark score.

The prediction is that the platform companies get in the queue. By the end of Q2 2027, at least one venture-funded company whose marketed core product is an autonomous or AI-driven penetration-testing platform, with Horizon3 the obvious candidate and not the only one, holds accreditation under CREST's new AI standards and appears as such in CREST's own accreditation listing. Four things do not count. General CREST penetration testing accreditation held without the new AI additions does not count, because it predates the question. A traditional consultancy that sells human engagements and has adopted an AI-assisted workflow does not count, because that is the constituency the standard was written for and its accreditation settles nothing about the platform companies. A blog post claiming alignment with the standard, a control-mapping document, or a signature on a voluntary code does not count, because independent assessment is the entire point of the thing. And an accreditation held by a services partner, reseller or delivery affiliate rather than by the platform company itself does not count, because routing the signature to somebody else is precisely the alternative outcome this rules out.

The strongest objection is that CREST accredits service providers, and a company selling a software subscription is not one, so the accreditation may simply not fit the corporate object being valued at two billion dollars. The second is geography: CREST's pull is heaviest in the United Kingdom, the Gulf and Singapore, and a US-anchored vendor selling into US enterprises may reasonably decide that its own certified staff and its customers' auditors are already enough. The third is the clock, since the standard is a week old, an assessment is not fast, and the window leaves about four quarters once a company decides to move. The fourth is the most interesting: this cuts against the story the round was priced on. A company that has just raised 250 million dollars arguing that offence and defence are both automated, and that is pushing from finding weaknesses into remediating them without a human in the loop, does not obviously want to advertise a standard whose founding premise is that a qualified human stays accountable throughout. What cuts the other way is who is standing on the other side of the trade. Microsoft's red agents probe the customer's own estate from inside it, its product page makes no compliance claim of any kind, and a platform vendor is not going to take onto its own paper the liability of an attested offensive engagement; it will sell the meter and leave the signature to partners. That leaves the signature as the one part of this category a bundle structurally cannot reach, and a company that just tripled its valuation has 250 million dollars with which to go and buy it.

reasoning.because: CREST opened AI-enabled pentest accreditation on July 28, six days before Horizon3's $250M round
reasoning.given: An auditor accepts a signature, not an exploit, and no bundled product ships an accountable tester
reasoning.so_that: A venture-funded autonomous-pentest platform company holds accreditation under CREST's new AI standards
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; in CREST's own accreditation listing, not a vendor marketing page
reasoning.plain_language: Firms selling automatic hacking tools will still get a human-run certificate, because auditors only accept a security test a qualified person signed.

predictions.summary: CREST opened the first accreditation for AI-enabled penetration testing on July 28, days before Horizon3 raised $250 million and Microsoft's red, blue and green agents reached preview. Compliance buys an accountable signature, not a capability. Expect a platform vendor accredited by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Agent-written accelerator stacks get an independent serving number by Q2 2027
predictions.body:
Jeremy Nixon, who left Google Brain to found Infinity last year, says his team pointed AI coding agents at d-Matrix silicon and had CUDA-equivalent software running in roughly ten hours, reaching about 92 percent of the Corsair part's theoretical peak on tensor-parallel matrix multiplication. Within ten days, he says, three frontier models were running end to end on the chip with every layer written from scratch. The agent doing the writing, Ignition, generates, tests and tunes the compute kernels that decide how efficiently an accelerator runs a model — historically the work that costs a challenger vendor a specialist team and several years, and the reason porting so rarely happens at all. Infinity closed a 15 million dollar seed at a 100 million valuation last month.

Every figure in that account is first-party, and the two claims inside it are not the same claim. Ninety-two percent of theoretical peak is a ratio against the arithmetic the silicon could in principle issue, measured on one kernel class, on a shape and a precision the kernel author selects, with the data already where it needs to be. That is a real engineering result and it is also the most flattering number available on a new part. End-to-end serving is a different measurement and a harder one: a named model at a stated precision, batch size and context length, carrying attention, key-value cache traffic, sampling, and the long tail of operators a matrix-multiply benchmark never touches. A stack can sit near peak on the kernel that matters most and still lose on tokens per second, because the operators nobody benchmarked are the ones that stall. Nixon's stronger claim — three models running end to end inside ten days — is the one that would settle the argument, and it arrived without a throughput figure beside it.

The same news cycle carried the disagreement about where the moat now sits. Rebellions' Marshall Choy says CUDA is no longer a factor for inference. Modular's Chris Lattner reads CUDA's graphics inheritance as a burden it cannot shed. Futurum's Daniel Newman points the other way, at NVIDIA's December purchase of SchedMD, which maintains the Slurm scheduler, and argues the moat moved up the stack rather than drained out of it. Argument does not resolve this. What resolves it is whether someone evaluating a challenger part can find a serving number they did not have to take from the seller.

So the prediction lands on who publishes, not on who is right. By the end of Q2 2027, a publicly readable artefact reports end-to-end inference throughput or latency for a named model running on a named non-NVIDIA accelerator whose kernel or compiler layer is stated to be machine-generated, and discloses the run configuration — model, precision, batch size or concurrency, sequence length — closely enough that a reader could attempt the same run. The publisher holds no commercial stake in either the silicon or the code generator: an academic group, an independent evaluation body, or a customer reporting its own measurement. One edge case is settled in advance rather than after the fact — a result carried in an MLCommons Inference round counts, even though the submitter runs the hardware, because the disclosure requirements and the review belong to the consortium and not to the submitter. How the stack was produced is irrelevant to the bar: an agent emitting Triton or MLIR counts exactly as much as an agent emitting hand-shaped kernels, provided the publication states that the layer was machine-written.

It resolves false if no artefact meeting all of those conditions is public on 30 June 2027, and there are three unremarkable ways that happens. The party best placed to run the measurement is the one selling the part, and independent evaluators tend to arrive after a buyer base exists rather than before it, so the whole corpus could still be vendor blogs, press releases, keynote slides and founder interviews, however detailed those get. Percent-of-peak has gravity of its own — it is cheap, it flatters, and it is what a seed-stage company can produce in a week — so the microbenchmark may simply keep being the number everyone quotes. The third route is worth naming because it is not a defeat for the underlying thesis: the field may settle on operator coverage as the honest metric, meaning how much of a framework's surface a generated stack actually implements, and report that in place of throughput. If that is what happens and no serving number appears from an unaffiliated publisher, this still resolves false.

reasoning.because: Infinity's 10-hour d-Matrix build and 92%-of-peak matmul figure are both first-party numbers
reasoning.given: Software, not silicon, kept challenger accelerators out; a moat claim only prices on outside proof
reasoning.so_that: A publisher with no stake in the silicon or the generator posts an end-to-end serving number, configuration disclosed
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; an independent publication, not a vendor blog or founder interview
reasoning.plain_language: A start-up says AI wrote chip software in ten hours. Someone with no stake has to measure it before it counts.

predictions.summary: A founder says AI agents wrote a CUDA-equivalent stack for d-Matrix silicon in about ten hours, at 92 percent of theoretical peak on matrix multiplication. Every figure is first-party. By Q2 2027 an unaffiliated publisher posts an end-to-end serving number for a machine-written stack.
